newsitem.title: USA: CME to halve size of S&P 500 index futures.
newsitem.headline: CME to halve size of S&P 500 index futures.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) board of directors decided to halve the size of the S&P 500 stock index futures contract, a CME spokesman said on Thursday.
The contract size would become $250 times the value of the index, he said. Currently, the multiplier is $500.
The move was aimed at making the contract "more easily accessible and more liquid," the spokesman said.
The change would have no effect on the level of index itself, the exchange said in a statement. It added that the effective size of options on S&P 500 futures would also remain unchanged.
The plan will now await approval by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, CME said.
Under the plan, the size of a S&P futures contract, with the underlying index at around 955, would be cut to about $238,000 from about $477,500 currently, the CME said.
When the futures began trading in 1982, the index was at about 116.5 and the contract size was about $58,200, it added.

"Equity and futures market alike have changed dramatically since the CME launched S&P 500 index futures in 1982," CME chairman Jack Sandner said in the statement. "Many investors and some funds have been priced out of S&P 500 futures as the market has skyrocketed to unprecedented levels."
With the current contract size, margin requirements to trade one contract could be more than $17,500.
To date, market participants had been split on the issue of cutting the contract size.
Opponents of the plan argued that large institutional investors would not be happy trading twice as many contracts and paying double the commissions to hedge what one contract hedges now.
The CME in June decided to launch a "mini" version of the S&P 500 futures, one-tenth the size of the existing contract, later in the year to attract smaller investors.
